idiom_name: session/context object registering new, dirty and removed objects + ordered flush in one transaction
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the application a session-scoped object that owns three collections - new, dirty and removed - keyed by database identity. Every mutation path registers its object (explicitly by calling a register method, or implicitly through instrumentation or a snapshot comparison at commit). The client opens a database transaction, does its business work, and calls commit once: the unit of work computes the statement set, orders it (inserts, then updates, then deletes, parents before children), executes it through the mappers, applies any optimistic version checks or locks, commits, and then clears its state. Keep per-table SQL in mappers and identity in an identity map; the unit of work itself must not know table structure.
code_sketch:
uow = UnitOfWork(connection)

with uow.transaction():                 # one business transaction
    order = uow.get(Order, id)          # identity map hit
    order.status = "paid"               # recorded as dirty
    uow.add(Audit(order.id, "paid"))   # recorded as new
    uow.remove(order.draft_lines)       # recorded as removed
# flush: inserts -> updates -> deletes, then COMMIT (ROLLBACK on error)
# uow.clear() afterwards; discard the uow entirely if it rolled back
pitfalls: Skipping registration on one mutation path (direct SQL, a raw statement, a second session): the change silently never reaches the flush.
Computing the flush order lazily without considering foreign keys, so the commit fails on constraint violations that the domain code never sees.
Reusing the unit of work after a rollback while its objects still carry the rolled-back changes.
Growing the unit of work into a cache or a service layer: it decides when to write, not what the business rules are.

Holding a database transaction open across external I/O calls (HTTP, message queue): the transaction holds a connection and any row locks for the duration of the external call — use the Transactional Outbox pattern instead.
Mixing AUTO-flush with mid-transaction queries: a JPQL query may flush all pending changes before executing, causing premature writes and unexpected lock acquisition.

Wrong move: relying on Doctrine ORM's flush to order UPDATEs safely -> its commit order follows entity hydration order, so two concurrent flushes touching the same rows take row locks in conflicting sequences and deadlock -> impose a deterministic update order (entity type, then id) or shrink the transaction (doctrine/orm issue #11345).

Wrong move: mutating a detached MikroORM entity and calling em.flush() expecting the write -> detached objects sit outside the UnitOfWork identity map, so no change set is computed and flush silently writes nothing -> re-attach with em.merge() or fetch/reference the entity in the current request context first.

Wrong move: enabling Django's ATOMIC_REQUESTS and assuming the Unit of Work is now in place -> each model.save() still executes SQL immediately inside the request transaction, so per-object round trips and unordered writes remain -> atomic() supplies atomicity only; deferred change tracking requires a unit-of-work ORM such as the SQLAlchemy Session.
